Ivanov is considered Chekhov's first full-length play to actually be staged, and critics and scholars have always treated it as a kind of rough draft for the masterworks that would follow: The Seagull, Uncle Vanya, Three Sisters, The Cherry Orchard. Notable productions of Ivanov over the years include a 2002 National Theatre production in London, and a 2008 staging featuring Kenneth Branagh and a young Tom Hiddleston. In New York, there was a 2012 staging at Classic Stage Company starring Ethan Hawke and a Lincoln Center Theatre production featuring Kevin Kline in 1997. And back in 1966, John Gielgud played Ivanov opposite Vivien Leigh. It is genuinely rarely produced, which makes this New American Ensemble production feel like a bit of a theatrical event for Chekhov lovers. So, what is Ivanov about? He married a woman named Anna, who was Jewish, and she converted to Christianity and was essentially disowned by her family so that she could be with him because she believed in him that much. And now, years later, he's a mess. He's in debt, his farm is failing, his wife is dying of tuberculosis, and he doesn't even know if he loves her anymore. He has completely lost all access to his own joy. He is, if we're being honest, clinically depressed. But this is 19th-century rural Russia, so there's no medication, no therapy, just a lot of vodka, card games, and people complaining about how bored they are. Around Ivanov swirls a colorful cast of characters: His scheming estate manager, Borkin; his buffoonish uncle, Count Shabelsky; the family he owes money to, the Lebedevs, whose daughter, Sasha, is desperately, hopelessly, youthfully in love with Ivanov. We have a pompous, self-righteous young doctor named Lvov, who is constantly moralizing at everyone, and a scene-stealing widow named Marta Babakina, who arrives looking like she wandered in from a slightly different, much louder play.
